sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: The Backup Light
case.hook: The jetty light is fixed. But a big storm is coming, and clouds will hide the Sun for days. Its solar panel can’t charge with no sunshine, so the keeper wants a backup light. My first try failed. Good! Now I know what to fix.

notice.head: NOTICE TO MARINERS · STORM WATCH
notice.title: CLOUDS AND STORM AHEAD
rows: ☁️ Thick clouds all day. Very little sunshine.
⛈️ Storm: strong wind, rain and salt spray.
The jetty light must shine every night.
notice.line: A forecast tells what the weather will probably do.

memo.t: Sam, the solar light can’t charge with no sunshine. Can you build a backup light that keeps shining through all of this? Work order attached.

case.question: What will make Sam’s backup light ready for the storm?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Criteria are the goals a design must meet. Constraints are the limits it must stay inside. Write both down first.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: limits cross out ideas
clues.t: The limits crossed out 4 of 6 ideas. Only ideas that fit the limits are worth building and testing.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: the version timeline
clues.t: Every failed test showed what to fix. Changing ONE thing at a time, Sam’s light got better: v1, v2, v3, v4.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: design it, then storm it
clues.t: A design isn’t ready until it passes a test in the real conditions: three cloudy days and a storm night.

solve.title: What will make the backup light ready for the storm?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Sam’s first design. Good engineers get it right on the first try.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Sam’s first try was too dim! It took four versions.

options.t: The brightest, biggest light, no matter what it costs.
options.why: Check Clue 1. The light has to stay inside the limits, like the budget.

options.t: A design that meets the goals, stays inside the limits, and passed a real storm test after redesigns.
options.why: Case cracked! Goals, limits, a test, and redesign until it passes: that’s engineering. Make your patent drawing just below.

options.t: Any design works if you build it carefully. You don’t need to test it.
options.why: Check Clue 4. Only a test in real conditions shows if it works.

stamps.q: What’s the difference between a criterion and a constraint?

opts.t: A criterion is a goal. A constraint is a limit.
They mean the same thing.
opts.miss: Look at your stamps. Are “seen from 1 mile” and “$50” the same kind of line?

opts.t: A constraint is a goal. A criterion is a limit.
opts.miss: Flip it! Which stamp did “Spend no more than $50” get?

stamps.win: Goals and limits, sorted. That’s step one for every engineer. Clue 1!

crossout.afterText: so you only test the good ones
crossout.title: Limits cross out ideas
todo: Add the keeper’s limits one at a time (press the button, or drag the next limit onto the ideas).
Watch which ideas get crossed out, and why.

why.t: Limits save time. Crossing out ideas that can’t work means you only build and test the good ones.

ideas.t: A long extension cord from shore

breaks.nobody: Someone has to light it every night.
Nobody is there to turn the crank.

ideas.t: A solar light with a bigger battery

limits.t: No wires out to the jetty.

crossout.dragLine: Or drag the next limit onto the ideas.
crossout.leftLine: Two ideas are left. Now they need testing!

opts.t: They crossed out ideas that couldn’t work, so only the good ones are left to test.
They picked the perfect design.
opts.miss: Two ideas are still left. Do we know yet which one works?

opts.t: They made the job impossible.
opts.miss: Look again. Are any ideas still standing?

crossout.win: 6 ideas, 3 limits, 2 left to test. Limits help! Clue 2!

versions.afterText: Watch Sam’s backup light change, version by version
versions.title: The version timeline
todo: Read the test results for each version of Sam’s wind-spinner light.
Pick the ONE change that fixes what failed.
Build and test the next version.

why.t: Each new try of a prototype. Engineers number them: v1, v2, v3… so they can compare.

versions.oneQ: What ONE change should Sam make for the next version?

crit.t: Survives a week of salt spray

vers.name: first try
vers.note: Too dim! From the boats, nobody could see it. Sam stopped testing here: no point testing the rest until it’s bright enough.

opts.t: Use a brighter LED.
Change everything: new spinner, new battery, new LED, new case.
opts.miss: If v2 works, how would Sam know WHICH change fixed it? Change ONE thing.

opts.t: Give up. Wind lights don’t work.
opts.miss: One failed test is information, not the end. What did the test tell Sam to fix?

vers.name: brighter LED
vers.note: Bright enough now! But at 2 AM the light went out. The brighter LED uses energy faster, and the small battery ran empty. Fixing one thing caused a new problem.

opts.t: Add a bigger battery.
Go back to the tiny LED.
opts.miss: Then it fails the brightness test again!

opts.t: Give up.
opts.miss: Sam is close! Which goal failed this time?

vers.name: bigger battery
vers.note: Bright, and it shines all night! But after 3 days of salt spray, the spinner’s motor rusted stuck. No spinning, no charging.

opts.t: Put the spinner’s motor in a salt-proof case.
Add an even bigger battery.
opts.miss: The battery was fine this time. Which goal failed?

opts.t: Paint the light a brighter color.
opts.miss: Paint won’t stop rust inside the motor. What failed?

vers.name: salt-proof case
parts: a small wind spinner in a salt-proof case
vers.note: All three goals pass! Four versions, one change at a time. Every failed test showed Sam what to fix next.

versions.q: Sam’s light failed three times. Was Sam a bad engineer?

opts.t: No. Each failed test showed what to fix, and the light got better every time.
Yes. Good engineers get it right the first time.
opts.miss: Look at the timeline. Did the failed tests help or hurt?

opts.t: Yes, Sam should have changed everything at once.
opts.miss: Then Sam wouldn’t know which change fixed what. One change at a time!

versions.win: Fail, learn, fix one thing, test again. That’s the design cycle! Clue 3!

stormtest.afterText: Build a backup light inside the keeper’s limits, then test it in the storm
stormtest.title: Design it, then storm it
todo: Pick ONE energy input and up to 2 add-ons. Stay under $50.
Press Run the storm test: 3 cloudy days, then a storm night.
If the light goes dark, read why, change your design and test again.

why.t: A light that works on a sunny day might fail when it matters most. Engineers test in the real conditions.

addons.note: Keeps salt spray off moving parts.
Brighter than needed. Uses more energy.
Catches a little more light on cloudy days.

stormtest.overLine: Over budget! The keeper’s limit is $50. Take something off.
stormtest.maxLine: Only 2 add-ons fit. Tap one to take it off first.

lines.dark: The battery ran empty and the light went dark.
lines.rust: Salt spray rusted the moving parts, so it stopped charging.
lines.person: Nobody was there at night to turn the crank.
lines.ok: The light shone every night, even in the storm!

stormtest.retryLine: Redesign: change ONE thing and test again.
stormtest.wow: The boats can see the jetty light all through the storm. Your design passed a real test.
stormtest.q: Why didn’t Sam trust the backup light until it passed the storm test?

opts.t: Only a test in the real conditions shows whether a design really works.
Because tests are fun.
opts.miss: They are fun! But what does a storm test SHOW?

opts.t: He didn’t need to. It looked good on paper.
opts.miss: Did every design that looked good on paper pass the storm?

stormtest.win: Tested in clouds and a storm, and it kept shining. Clue 4!

photos.title: They failed first, too

fold.tease: A real 1901 photo: the famous airplane builders had a glider that disappointed them. What did they do next?

todo: Tap each number on the photo.

why.t: Wilbur and Orville Wright, two bike makers from Ohio. In 1903 they flew the first powered airplane.

photos.alt: An old black-and-white photo: a big two-winged glider made of cloth and wood floats above the sand, held by ropes. Two men stand on the beach holding the ropes.
photos.credit: 1901 Wright glider flown as a kite at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina: photo by Wilbur or Orville Wright, Library of Congress (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

hotspots.label: The wings
hotspots.t: In 1901 these wings lifted much less than the Wrights’ numbers said they should. A disappointing test!

hotspots.label: The ropes
hotspots.t: They flew it like a kite first, with nobody on it. A safe way to test a prototype.

hotspots.label: The sand
hotspots.t: Kitty Hawk has steady wind and soft sand for landings. A good place to test.

task.q: Match each clue to a number on the photo.
task.win: After this test, the Wrights built a small wind tunnel and tested more than 200 model wings. Their redesigned 1902 glider made hundreds of good glides. Failing first helped them succeed.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how to design a device that converts energy?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Engineers set goals and limits, test a prototype, and redesign it when a test fails.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “goals and limits”, “test a prototype” and “redesign”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
